title: RBA admits ‘a lot has to go right’ to avoid another hike
full_text:
With so many variables at play, the Reserve Bank is still leaning towards a fourth rate rise.
RBA assistant governor Chris Kent has reinforced the hawkish message from policymakers, saying that “a lot of things still have to go right” to get inflation back inside the 2-3 per cent target band by the end of 2027 as the RBA has forecast.
In a speech at an event in Sydney, Kent repeated the board’s assessment that policy was “somewhat restrictive” after its three rate rises since February.
But while the RBA has raised the cash rate back up to its post-Covid high amid an inflation resurgence exacerbated by the Iran war, policymakers aren’t sure if they have done enough.
“I think the risks that the board are focused very much on are that a few of the sorts of things in our forecasts, quite a few of those things have to go right in order to ensure that inflation does come back down,” Kent said.
While an unexpected demand shock “might do some of that job” in terms of lowering inflation, the Iran war and subsequent supply shock from the Middle East was a “very challenging circumstance” for monetary policy as it “worsens very much the trade-off between unemployment and inflation”, he added.
Governor Michele Bullock was clear on Tuesday that the board was in “wait and see” mode.
But it was a bit surprising that that the board considered a rate rise simply because three months had passed. In the end, the decision to keep interest rates on hold was unanimous.
But even with lower than expected inflation, higher than expected unemployment and a sharp fall in house prices since their last meeting, the fact that the board formally considered a rate rise this month suggests its reaction function remains skewed in a hawkish direction.
The board also considered a rate rise even after the slight downward revisions to near-term inflation forecasts by the RBA. Those tweaks were made even with the assumption that the cash rate peaks at 4.5 per cent next year, rather than 4.7 per cent previously expected.
Rather than highlight any disinflationary signal from the economic data or house prices since June, Bullock said “what’s keeping us on hold is that we’ve already raised three times”.
“We think we’ve got tight financial conditions, but we need a bit more evidence on whether we’re tight enough to get inflation back down and to ease the excess capacity we’ve got in the economy. The sharp fall in house prices didn’t stop the board from considering another hike.” Kent also highlighted various forces pulling the inflation outlook in different directions.
He said housing market conditions had “softened noticeably” in recent months, while growth of new housing loans had “fallen significantly” and forward indicators such as auction clearance rates had also “declined to be below their long-run averages”.
Some of the downturn was due to higher interest rates and a pullback after a long period of very strong growth in housing prices. But the tax changes announced in the federal budget “appear to have contributed to reduced demand in the established housing market by lowering the after-tax return from housing for investors”.
“All else equal, these changes will tend to reduce the extent to which monetary policy needs to constrain the growth in aggregate demand to help bring inflation back to the RBA’s target,” Kent said.
But another important development potentially working in the opposite direction in terms of its impact on economic activity and inflation has been the resilience of the growth in aggregate demand globally associated with “sizeable AI-related investments”.
“Substantial investment in data centres and AI-related infrastructure has helped to support growth in aggregate demand of late,” Kent said.
“This is most obvious in economies driving AI innovation and manufacturing, including the US, South Korea and Taiwan. It is also occurring in Australia, though to a lesser extent.” This “AI activity” meant “policy rates need to be higher than otherwise, at least in the short run.” Kent said this would also be reflected in government bond yields, and to the extent that yields rise by more offshore than in Australia, this would tend to imply a lower value for the dollar.
And given that the exchange rate is a key part of the transmission of monetary policy, at the margin this means that a given level of the cash rate is less restrictive than it would otherwise be.
In addition to this effect, large public debts and deficits are contributing to higher government bond yields in Europe, Japan and the US which would tend to weigh on the Australian dollar exchange rate in a similar way to the effect of strong AI-related investment on aggregate demand offshore. “Rising government deficits have also been cited as a factor contributing to the rise in global neutral rates over recent years, a trend which has reduced the tightness of Australian financial conditions for a given level of the cash rate,” Kent said.
